lead: An avionics architecture is the plan of where computing happens and how data moves between sensors, computers and displays. Older aircraft use a federated architecture: one box per function, each with its own wiring. Newer aircraft use integrated modular avionics (IMA): a few shared cabinets host many functions as protected software partitions. In both, the hardware is packaged as line replaceable units (LRUs) that a technician can swap on the apron, and built-in test tells the technician which one to swap.
prereq: You need: Civil, military, spacecraft and UAV avionics for the building blocks and the redundancy targets.

blocks.text: A line replaceable unit (LRU) is a sealed box that can be removed and replaced on the flight line with hand tools and a short functional test, without a hangar visit. Each LRU has a part number, a connector, a mounting tray in the avionics bay and its own self-test. Inside it are shop replaceable units (circuit cards) that only a workshop opens.

In a federated architecture each function owns its own LRU. The air data computer works out airspeed and altitude, the inertial reference unit gives attitude and heading, and the autopilot computer sends commands to the servo actuators that move the control surfaces. Boxes exchange data on dedicated links, usually ARINC 429 on civil aircraft and MIL-STD-1553B on military ones (see Data buses: ARINC 429 and MIL-STD-1553B).

items: Strength: a fault stays inside one box, so it is easy to find and easy to certify.
Strength: each supplier designs and qualifies its box alone.
Weakness: every new function adds a box with its own power supply, case, cooling and wiring, so mass, power and connector count grow with the number of functions.
Weakness: an airline must stock many different spare part numbers.

sections.h3: IMA: shared cabinets, modules and partitions

blocks.text: Integrated modular avionics (IMA) replaces many single-function boxes with a few cabinets or racks. A cabinet holds plug-in modules: core processing modules, input/output modules and power supply modules, joined by a backplane (a board that carries power and data between them). Remote data concentrators near the sensors turn analog signals into digital words, so long analog wire runs disappear. Examples are the shared cabinets of the Boeing 777, the IMA of the Airbus A380 and A350, and the Common Core System of the Boeing 787.

Each hosted function runs in a partition. ARINC 653 is the software standard that defines it. A partition gets a fixed window of processor time in a repeating major frame, and its own memory area protected by hardware. One function therefore cannot overwrite another function's data or steal its time, even if it crashes. This is called robust partitioning, and it is what allows a less critical function to share a processor with a critical one.

blocks.where: U is the processor utilisation in per cent; tᵢ is the time window of partition i in ms; T<sub>MF</sub> is the major frame in ms. Each partition runs once per major frame, so its rate is 1 ÷ T<sub>MF</sub>.

blocks.text: Redundancy does not go away with IMA. One module may now carry several functions, so one module fault is a common-mode fault. Designers place the two copies of a critical function on modules in different cabinets with separate power, and keep standby modules.

Built-in test equipment (BITE) is the circuitry and software inside each LRU or module that checks it. Power-up BITE runs when power is applied, continuous BITE runs in flight, and initiated BITE runs on command from a maintenance terminal. Fault codes are stored in non-volatile memory and sent to a central maintenance computer, which can also downlink them before landing, so a technician can meet the aircraft with the right spare.

examples.question: An aircraft carries 8 federated LRUs, each of mass 2 kg and drawing 40 W. An IMA cabinet that hosts all eight functions has a total mass of 5 kg and draws 90 W. Find the mass and power saved, and express each as a percentage of the federated value.
steps: Federated mass: 8 × 2 kg = 16 kg. Federated power: 8 × 40 W = 320 W.
examples.answer: The cabinet saves 11 kg (68.75 %) and 230 W (about 71.9 %). Less power also means less heat for the avionics cooling system to remove.

examples.question: An IMA core module runs ARINC 653 partitions in a 50 ms major frame: flight management 20 ms, display management 12 ms, fuel quantity 8 ms and maintenance 5 ms. (a) Find the utilisation and the spare time. (b) At what rate does each partition run? (c) Can a new 8 ms cabin function be added to this module?
steps: Each partition runs once per major frame: rate = 1 ÷ 0.050 s = 20 Hz.
New function: it needs 8 ms but only 5 ms is free, and 45 + 8 = 53 ms is more than 50 ms. It does not fit.
Options: host it on another module, or shorten another window only if that function's own timing analysis still passes.
examples.answer: Utilisation 90 % with 5 ms spare; every partition runs at 20 Hz; the 8 ms function does not fit, because 53 ms exceeds the 50 ms major frame.

traps: Writing that IMA removes redundancy. Shared hardware creates common-mode faults, so critical functions are split across modules and cabinets.
Calling a circuit card an LRU. The LRU is the box swapped on the apron; cards inside it are shop replaceable units.
Confusing ARINC 653 (partitioning in software) with ARINC 429 or ARINC 664 (data on a wire).
Adding partition windows and forgetting that the total must fit inside one major frame.
Saying BITE proves the system healthy. It tests its own box; wiring and neighbouring units can still be at fault.

quiz.q: Define an LRU and name what sits inside it.
quiz.a: A box that can be removed and replaced on the flight line with hand tools and a short test. Inside it are shop replaceable units (circuit cards).
Power-up BITE, continuous (in-flight) BITE and initiated BITE from a maintenance terminal.

quiz.q: How does ARINC 653 stop one partition from disturbing another?
quiz.a: Time partitioning gives each partition a fixed window in the major frame, and memory partitioning gives it a protected memory area. A failing partition cannot take extra time or write into another's memory.

quiz.q: Why does federated mass grow with every added function?
quiz.a: Each function brings its own box, power supply, case, cooling path and point-to-point wiring; nothing is shared.

quiz.q: Six LRUs of 3 kg and 30 W each are replaced by a 4 kg, 70 W cabinet. Find the mass and power saved.
quiz.a: Federated: 18 kg and 180 W. Saved: 18 − 4 = 14 kg and 180 − 70 = 110 W.

quiz.q: A 25 ms major frame holds partitions of 6, 9 and 4 ms. Find the utilisation and the rate of each partition.
A display function of high criticality shares a module with a cabin function of no safety effect. What must the designer show?
quiz.a: That robust partitioning holds: the cabin partition cannot overrun its time window or write into the display partition's memory, and a crash of the cabin partition leaves the display partition running. The module and its operating system must be assured to the higher level.

quiz.q: BITE reports no fault, yet a display shows a wrong value. Give two reasons.
quiz.a: The fault may be in wiring, a connector or another unit that this BITE does not test; or the unit may be drifting but still inside its BITE limits.

beyond: Not for the exam. Second-generation IMA aims to let one cabinet type serve many aircraft programmes, and open architectures let software from one supplier run on another supplier's module. Multicore processors make partitioning harder, because cores share caches and memory paths; certification guidance now covers this interference. Search for 'ARINC 653', 'remote data concentrator', 'Boeing 787 Common Core System' and 'multicore interference avionics'.
